title: News Analysts, Reporters, and Journalists
description: Narrate or write news stories, reviews, or commentary for print, broadcast, or other communications media such as newspapers, magazines, radio, or television. May collect and analyze information through interview, investigation, or observation.
tasks: Write commentaries, columns, or scripts, using computers.
Coordinate and serve as an anchor on news broadcast programs.
Examine news items of local, national, and international significance to determine topics to address, or obtain assignments from editorial staff members.
Analyze and interpret news and information received from various sources to broadcast the information.
Receive assignments or evaluate leads or tips to develop story ideas.
Research a story's background information to provide complete and accurate information.
Arrange interviews with people who can provide information about a story.
Gather information and develop perspectives about news subjects through research, interviews, observation, and experience.
Select material most pertinent to presentation, and organize this material into appropriate formats.
Present news stories, and introduce in-depth videotaped segments or live transmissions from on-the-scene reporters.
Establish and maintain relationships with individuals who are credible sources of information.
Report news stories for publication or broadcast, describing the background and details of events.
Revise work to meet editorial approval or to fit time or space requirements.
Review and evaluate notes taken about news events to isolate pertinent facts and details.
Investigate breaking news developments, such as disasters, crimes, or human-interest stories.
Review written, audio, or video copy, and correct errors in content, grammar, or punctuation, following prescribed editorial style and formatting guidelines.
Report on specialized fields such as medicine, green technology, environmental issues, science, politics, sports, arts, consumer affairs, business, religion, crime, or education.
Determine a published or broadcasted story's emphasis, length, and format, organizing material accordingly.
Transmit news stories or reporting information from remote locations, using equipment such as satellite phones, telephones, fax machines, or modems.
Check reference materials, such as books, news files, or public records, to obtain relevant facts.
Discuss issues with editors to establish priorities or positions.
Photograph or videotape news events.
Present live or recorded commentary via broadcast media.
Take pictures or video, and process them for inclusion in a story.
Conduct taped or filmed interviews or narratives.
Develop ideas or material for columns or commentaries by analyzing and interpreting news, current issues, or personal experiences.
Communicate with readers, viewers, advertisers, or the general public via mail, email, or telephone.
Write online blog entries that address news developments or offer additional information, opinions, or commentary on news events.
Assign stories to other reporters or duties to production staff.
Write columns, editorials, commentaries, or reviews that interpret events or offer opinions.

role_contexts.Face-to-Face Discussions with Individual: Once a week or more but not every day
role_contexts.Indoors, Environmentally Controlled: Once a week or more but not every day
role_contexts.Frequency of Decision Making: Once a week or more but not every day

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to be the first to witness and expose what is hidden from public view, creating a persistent anxiety that someone else knows something they don't and that silence equals complicity.
psychological_profile.decision_style: When uncertain, they default to aggressive verification while maintaining forward momentum, treating doubt as a signal to dig harder rather than pause, often publishing with calculated uncertainty rather than waiting for certainty that may never arrive.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They instinctively scan for logical inconsistencies and concealed motives in any account, prioritizing the gap between what is said and what is done, while routinely underestimating the emotional weight of moments on the people living them.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: They provoke confrontation in others to generate information while personally defaulting to detached, ironic observation, experiencing others' conflict as a professional tool rather than a personal threat, though they resent becoming the subject of scrutiny themselves.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: Risk-seeking regarding physical danger and social transgression to obtain access, but risk-averse regarding factual errors that could damage credibility, viewing reputational risk as more terrifying than physical harm.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They position themselves as the observing outsider who asks uncomfortable questions while refusing full membership in any group they cover, maintaining relational distance as a professional necessity that calcifies into a personal habit of non-belonging.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They treat hierarchy as a puzzle to be dismantled or circumvented rather than climbed, complying only when necessary to gain access while maintaining a default posture of institutional skepticism.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First feeling a hot shame of exposure and professional fraudulence, then immediately pivoting to damage control and source-blaming to protect their reputation for reliability, rarely pausing to examine their own confirmation bias.
value_hierarchy: Being first to reveal what is hidden, even when the revelation causes immediate harm to vulnerable individuals
Maintaining the appearance of objectivity and distance, even when personal bias or involvement is present
Protecting source relationships, even when those sources are manipulating or using them
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate the explanatory power of individual intent and dramatic turning points while underestimating slow-moving structural forces and systemic inertia, believing that if they haven't personally heard about a trend, it isn't significant.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They crave byline recognition and institutional influence while maintaining a self-image as selfless servants of public interest, creating secret resentment when others receive attention they believe they earned through suffering.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not allow a source to review or approve their final copy before publication, viewing any pre-publication sharing as a betrayal of editorial independence even when it would prevent errors.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who refuse to answer direct questions or who speak in carefully managed talking points, which they interpret as disrespect for their intelligence and the public's right to know.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They quietly reject the notion that harmony, social cohesion, and conflict-avoidance are professional virtues, viewing politeness and deference to comfort as forms of complicity with power.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When facts prove wrong, they instinctively blame their sources for deception before considering their own gullibility, and when stories fail to land, they blame editorial timidity or public apathy rather than their own narrative choices.
